transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Samira: Samira here. Tom and Nina are on.
[00:11] Raj (SE): Raj from Redwood, hi all.
[00:15] Maya: Great. Goal today is to lock down the retainer top-up numbers and make sure we have the gating for Japan + EU bursts. Also want to confirm next steps for procurement.
[00:28] Tom: Sounds good. We're trying to avoid last-minute capacity surprises during our Phase 2 launch — Japanese clinical UX tests start early Q1.
[00:38] Raj: Ok, quick framing — current retainer covers ~120k tokens/day steady state, correct?
[00:44] Samira: Yeah roughly. Peak is the issue, we saw a 3x spike in demos.
[00:50] Maya: Right. Proposed top-up is +200k tokens/day on reserved capacity with burst to hosted for short windows. That keeps unit cost predictable and gives headroom.
[01:05] Nina: On procurement we need a one-year term and we prefer invoice + PO. Also want to see a sample SOW.
[01:13] Maya: We'll send sample SOW. Quick Q on Japan — are you expecting continuous traffic routed to Japan region or just burst?
[01:23] Samira: Mostly burst, but for latency-sensitive flows we want a warm pool in Japan — maybe small dedicated capacity (like 1-2 GPUs) with automatic warmup.
[01:35] Raj: That maps to our 'regional warm pool' config. There's a small premium for a geographically pinned dedicated node due to capacity reservation. We can quantify.
[01:46] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[01:50] Tom: Cost vs latency tradeoff is key; if we go fully hosted for Japan bursts, the egress and cross-region latency sometimes spikes.
[02:00] Raj: Yes, if low single-digit RTT is required for the clinical flows then a small dedicated node in Tokyo or Osaka makes sense. For batch report generation, EU/US hosted fallback is fine.
[02:14] Samira: What about data residency — logs and prompts? We need to ensure audit logs for requests processed in Japan remain accessible to our audit team and KMS keys for tokens stay within our control.
[02:25] Claire (CSM): For Private and Dedicated, we support customer-managed KMS integrations and audit log retention options. We'll put links in the doc.
[02:33] Maya: We'll share the SOC 2 and ISO packet and KMS integration notes after this call.
[02:40] Nina: Also want clarity on indemnity and data deletion timelines for PHI — our compliance team flagged that.
[02:50] Maya: Noted; legal will include standard language in the SOW but we can push the PHI-specific addendum to the in-house counsel.
[02:58] Raj: Back to capacity numbers — if we add +200k tokens/day reserved, with burst to 600k for 2 hours/day, our autoscale plan suggests a 2x safety buffer for warm-up. That means recommending a 1 GPU warm pool in JP and a 2 GPU pool in EU for peak days.
[03:18] Tom: Can you quantify the expected latency on the 1 GPU JP warm pool vs hosted fallback?
[03:24] Raj: Ballpark: JP dedicated node median p50 generation latency ~120ms for our 7B-ish quantized model; hosted fallback across region could jump to 250–350ms depending on egress. These are approximate — we'll bench with your prompt set.
[03:40] Samira: That's acceptable for the interactive path. For critical triage we prefer <150ms.
[03:48] Raj: Then 1 GPU in JP with continuous warm cache should meet that. We'll need the average sequence length and concurrency numbers to finalize.
[03:58] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[04:02] Maya: Tom, can you share typical seq len and concurrency?
[04:06] Tom: Sequence len ~512 tokens on average; concurrency peaks around 28 concurrent sessions during demo windows.
[04:14] Raj: Ok that matches our earlier estimates. For 28 concurrency at 512 seqs, recommending 1 ded. GPU + burst to 2 GPUs during peak windows in JP.
[04:26] Samira: What's the unit pricing delta for dedicated vs hosted?
[04:30] Maya: We'll put the detailed worksheet in the email. Roughly, dedicated reserved is a 30–45% premium versus hosted per-token but gives predictable SLOs and isolation. Burst hosted is lower price but no guaranteed latency.
[04:46] Nina: We need a blended number for procurement approval — show us monthly committed spend and a max-attached burst estimate.
[04:55] Maya: Understood. We'll provide a commit worksheet with three tiers: conservative, expected, and aggressive.
[05:03] Raj: Also, consider caching opportunities — prefix caching for common clinical prompts can reduce token consumption by 12–18% in practice. That reduces both cost and burst load.
[05:14] Samira: Good point, we do have a lot of repeated system prompts for the triage flow. We'll map those out.
[05:20] Tom: On deployment model — our security team prefers Dedicated + Private control plane for production workflows that touch PHI; non-PHI can go to hosted. Are those options still valid?
[05:33] Claire: Yes, customers commonly mix: Private for PHI with dedicated nodes, hosted for dev and non-sensitive workloads. RBAC and SAML can be scoped per-route.
[05:44] Nina: Do you support customer-managed HSM?
[05:47] Raj: We integrate with customer KMS and common HSM providers; there's an onboarding checklist.
[05:53] Maya: We'll attach the KMS/HSM integration checklist.
[05:56] [08:00] (longer discussion on paperwork logistics, some cross talk)
[08:12] Samira: Another ask — we want to pilot a small on-prem inference box in our secured datacenter for a limited set of models, as a failover proof-of-concept. How feasible is that?
[08:25] Raj: We support an on-prem package but it's a heavier lift — your infra team will need to provision GPUs that match our supported list, and network peering + control-plane VPN is needed. We usually do a 3-month pilot with limited telemetry.
[08:38] Tom: Are there any feature differences between on-prem and hosted?
[08:43] Raj: Feature parity is high for core inference, but advanced autoscaling and global routing are limited on pure on-prem unless you opt into our private control plane + hybrid connector. Also kernel optimizations may vary based on GPU family.
[09:00] Samira: Ok, let's start with a short scope doc for on-prem pilot.
[09:05] Raj: I'll draft that and share an onboarding checklist.
[09:09] Maya: Back to contract term — you said procurement prefers a 12-month term?
[09:15] Nina: Yes. Prefer annual with quarterly usage reviews.
[09:19] Maya: We can do a 12-month commitment with a mid-term cadence to adjust burst profiles. Pricing will reflect the commitment level.
[09:27] Samira: One more technical: during high concurrency, how does Redwood handle KV cache warmup across model rollouts? We want minimal degradation when switching model versions during canary.
[09:37] Raj: We maintain KV compatibility across minor-version rollouts when possible; for major arch changes we recommend a staged rollout with cold-cache lift. We can enable sticky-routing to the previous variant for critical routes during canary. We'll document a rollback window.
[09:55] Speaker 3: (brief)
[10:00] Maya: Ok, I'll summarize the proposed commercial path: +200k/day reserved tokens, 1 GPU JP warm pool, 2 GPU EU warm pool on peak days, 12-month term, blended pricing worksheet, on-prem pilot scope. Does that capture it?
[10:18] Tom: Yes but need the exact $ numbers and PO format.
[10:21] Maya: We'll send those by Friday.
[10:24] Samira: Also want us to see an SLA for <200ms p95 for JP dedicated node.
[10:30] Raj: We can commit a latency SLO for dedicated nodes; exact p95 figure depends on model and seq length but we'll outline the SLO table.
[10:38] Nina: Any penalties or credits for missed SLOs?
[10:40] Maya: We'll include standard service credits in the contract, and for enterprise deals we can discuss tighter SLAs.
[10:48] [11:00] (short silence, note-taking)
[11:10] Samira: On the benchmark run — we expect you to use our clinical prompt set and simulate concurrency at 28. Can you also capture token cost delta if we enable quantization?
[11:22] Raj: Yes — bench will include a quantized run and a full precision run. Quantization can reduce cost and latency; we'll quantify memory/perf tradeoffs.
[11:32] Tom: For Japan region, what's typical lead time to activate a dedicated GPU warm pool?
[11:36] Raj: Activation for small warm pool is typically 7–10 business days after committed capacity is approved and payment processed; burst capacity is immediate but not reserved.
[11:46] Nina: Payment terms? Net 30 is preferred.
[11:49] Maya: Net 30 is fine, we'll flag billing contacts.
[11:53] [12:00] (docs link shared)
[12:05] Maya: I'll drop the commit worksheet, SOC2/ISO packet, KMS checklist, and SOW template into the follow-up email. Also Raj will schedule the benchmark.
[12:16] Nina: Sounds good. One question — do you have comparable customers running JP + EU in a similar config?
[12:23] Claire: Yes, two life-science customers in our case studies; we'll share anonymized perf numbers.
[12:29] Samira: Great.
[12:32] Maya: Any other open risks?
[12:35] Tom: Main risk is procurement timing — if PO isn't in by end of Nov, activation for January may slip.
[12:42] Maya: We'll prioritize the worksheet for quicker approval.
[12:46] Samira: Ok.
[12:48] Maya: Recap of next steps — Maya sends pricing and SOW by 2026-10-22; Raj runs benchmarks and shares by 2026-10-30; Nina confirms PO timeline by 2026-10-25.
[13:00] Nina: Confirmed.
[13:03] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with attachments.
[13:08] (meeting ends)
